evidence.title: P. G. Wodehouse
evidence.text: Born in Guildford, the son of a British magistrate based in Hong Kong, Wodehouse spent happy teenage years at Dulwich College, to which he remained devoted all his life.

evidence.title: P. G. Wodehouse
evidence.text: After leaving school he was employed by a bank but disliked the work and turned to writing in his spare time.

evidence.title: P. G. Wodehouse

evidence.title: P. G. Wodehouse
evidence.text: They include the jolly gentleman of leisure Bertie Wooster and his sagacious valet, Jeeves; the immaculate and loquacious Psmith; Lord Emsworth and the Blandings Castle set; the Oldest Member, with stories about golf; and Mr Mulliner, with tall tales on subjects ranging from bibulous bishops to megalomaniac movie moguls.

evidence.title: Losing Nelson
evidence.text: Losing Nelson is a 1999 novel by Barry Unsworth.

evidence.title: Losing Nelson
evidence.text: Its protagonist is Charles Cleasby, who is obsessed with Lord Nelson, attempts to re-enact events of "Horatio"'s life to the point of feeling that he is the admiral, and who is writing a hagiographic biography.

evidence.title: Losing Nelson
evidence.text: His typist, the down-to-earth Miss Lily, serves as his foil in her criticism of Nelson's ego and treatment of his wife.

evidence.title: Losing Nelson
evidence.text: At the end, when Cleasby has journeyed to Naples to do research in the hope of exonerating his hero for his execution of Admiral Caracciolo and other Neapolitan Jacobins, he murders a child near the location of Nelson's betrayal, simultaneously imagining that he is killing the child Nelson and that the act forever merges him with Nelson.
